info.bio:
Pearl Jam es una banda de rock, procedentes de Seattle, y uno de los líderes del movimiento grunge a principios de la década de los 90s. A pesar del hecho de que otros grupos de dicho movimiento han desaparecido Pearl Jam se mantiene estabilizado en un puesto predominante dentro del mundo musical, después de veinte años de carrera y nueve álbumes grabados en estudio hasta la fecha.
Se considera a su vocalista, Eddie Vedder, como una de las mejores voces del rock contemporáneo.

scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Nevermind de Nirvana (noviembre de 1991) llega al número uno el 11 de enero de 1992 y acaba con el reinado del lite metal. Los medios abrazan a Kurt Cobain y Eddie Vedder, las radios crean formatos «alternativos», la gran emisora de metal de Los Ángeles, KNAC, se vende en 1995 y MTV cancela Headbangers Ball en 1996; hasta Kerrang! se abre a la nueva moda, y los críticos, que crecieron con el rock universitario, ven por fin validado su gusto. El grunge no es metal aunque comparte la guitarra y la voz fuerte: alterna partes duras y suaves, canta el dolor y la desesperación, viste de tienda de segunda mano e identifica a la generación X con los débiles, frente al poder y el placer del metal («Somos pesados, pero no heavy metal», dice Krist Novoselic). Hacia 1998 el alternativo está moribundo.

scenes.desc: El grunge, revival del hard rock de los setenta y renacimiento musical de Seattle, fue uno de los grandes fenómenos de los noventa (casi solo en EE UU). Green River lo inauguran (Come On Down) y Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Melvins y Mudhoney fijan sus cuatro puntos cardinales; Nirvana, con Nevermind, lo convierten en una tragaperras y en la banda sonora de la crisis nerviosa de una generación. Después, Alice In Chains (Dirt), Foo Fighters, Hammerbox, GodHeadSilo, Everclear, Stone Temple Pilots, Tool (el grupo más innovador de la segunda generación: Aenima, Lateralus), God Machine, Helmet, Quicksand, Urge Overkill, los Smashing Pumpkins (Siamese Dream, Mellon Collie), Scarce, Creed, Bush, Manic Street Preachers, Silverchair.

podcast.title: Formation Origin - Pickup Basketball Game (1989)
podcast.body: The band's genesis began in Seattle when Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament formed Love Company and sought a singer by circulating a demo. Jack Irons, a former Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer, received a copy of this demo and passed it to Eddie Vedder, a surfer and night shift worker at a Chevron tank farm in San Diego, after a pickup basketball game in 1989. Eddie then wrote lyrics to three of the demo's five songs, dubbed them onto a new cassette, and sent it to Seattle, leading to his invitation to jam with the group and the formation of Pearl Jam. "This cassette passed out of a gym bag sometime in 1989 might have resulted in the most profitable pickup basketball game ever played."

podcast.title: Escalating Threats and Suicide Talk (Nov-Dec 1990)
podcast.body: In November 1990, Jeremy Dell began casually discussing suicide with classmates. The following month, he was again on in-school suspension for making more threats against teachers, had stolen money from a cash box at a basketball game, continued talking about suicide, and made a specific threat about "blowing the head off a particular teacher." These incidents marked a clear escalation of his troubling behavior and mental state. "The following month, he was back on in-school suspension for making more threats against teachers."

podcast.title: Jeremy Dell's Suicide Attempts (April-June 1990)
podcast.body: Between April and June 1990, Jeremy Dell attempted suicide at least three times, utilizing different methods including pills, threatening to jump off a church roof, and making threats to shoot himself. This history indicated a clear need for additional help and treatment that he evidently did not receive. "Between April and June 1990, he attempted suicide at least three times, pills, threatening to jump off the roof of a church, and a threat to shoot himself."

podcast.title: Formation and Early Days (1991)
podcast.body: During the filming of *Singles* in early 1991, Pearl Jam had "barely been born." Eddie Vedder had recently moved from San Diego to Seattle and was "hanging out with his future bandmates," indicating they were in the very nascent stages of their formation, predating the grunge explosion. "As Singles started filling, Pearl Jam had barely been born, although Eddie Vetter had already moved from San Diego to Seattle where he was hanging out with his future bandmates."

podcast.title: The Day of Jeremy Dell's Suicide (January 8, 1991)
podcast.body: On the morning of Tuesday, January 8, 1991, Jeremy Dell woke at 7:10 AM, called a friend, Nancy, and mentioned he was already high from smoking weed, appearing happy. He arrived at Richardson High at 8:20 AM and gave other students a letter to be mailed, stating he wouldn't be around after school. After missing his 9 AM class, he arrived late to his second-period English class at 9:35 AM. When teacher Fay Barnette followed procedure to send him to the principal's office for a late slip, Jeremy instead went to his locker (number 540), retrieved the stolen .357 Magnum, returned to the classroom, placed his hall pass on the teacher's desk, and, turning to her, stated, "Miss, I got what I really went for." He then put the gun in his mouth and pulled the trigger in front of approximately 30 classmates, with the bang heard throughout the school. "He then got out the gun, put it in his mouth, and pulled the trigger. There were about 30 other kids in the room at the time."

podcast.title: 1992 Seattle Free Show Ticketing Dispute
podcast.body: In May 1992, Pearl Jam planned a free show in Seattle for approximately 30,000 people and approached Ticketmaster to handle the ticketing, as city requirements mandated monitoring the crowd size. Ticketmaster quoted costs of $1 to $1.50 per ticket, which would amount to $45,000 for the band to absorb. Pearl Jam ultimately decided not to use Ticketmaster for this event, a decision that marked the beginning of their significant conflict with the ticketing giant. "In the end, for this particular show, Pearl Jam elected not to use ticket master, but the experience somehow left a bad taste in their mouth. And this was the beginning of a fight."

podcast.title: Bile Beer Drinking Contest – 1992 Lollapalooza, Jim Rose Circus, Matt "the Tube" Crowley
podcast.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would swallow a seven-foot hose connected to a hand pump, force beer, ketchup, mustard, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach, then pump it all back out into glasses for audience members to drink. At one stop on the tour featuring both Pearl Jam and Soundgarden, Eddie Vedder and Chris Cornell entered a competition to see who could consume the most of this bile cocktail. Eddie won decisively and named his victory "Wayne." "Eddie won this contest. He called it Wayne."

podcast.title: Cameo in Singles (1992)
podcast.body: Pearl Jam made a cameo appearance in the 1992 Hollywood motion picture *Singles*. The film was significant for not only featuring the music of the moment but also including appearances from prominent bands and figures of the burgeoning alternative and grunge scene, helping to expand grunge's reach. "It was a Hollywood motion picture that not only featured the music of the moment, but also cameos from Pearl Jam and Chris Cornell and Allison Chains."

podcast.title: Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell, and Al Jourgensen – Bile Beer Drinking Contest at Lollapalooza 1992
podcast.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including performer Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would pump beer, ketchup, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach via a seven-foot swallowed tube and then pump it back out as "bile beer" for audience members to drink. Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell (Soundgarden), and Al Jourgensen (Ministry) entered a competition for who could drink the most bile beer. Cornell tried and retched; Jourgensen managed it two days in a row; Eddie was there every single night and claimed to have drunk two quarts more than anyone. When asked why, Eddie said: "Just looking for attention." "Eddie won this contest. He called it Wayne."

podcast.title: Popularity in Late 1992
podcast.body: By late summer 1992, Pearl Jam's popularity had surged, contributing to the success of Temple of the Dog, a side project they collaborated on in 1991. The tribute album broke into the top 10 of the album chart and belatedly achieved platinum status. "By the late summer of 92, both Pearl Jam and Soundgarden were so popular with new fans hungry for new material that a tiny side project they'd collaborated on back in 1991 called Temple of the Dog."

podcast.body: In Cameron Crowe's Seattle-set film *Singles* (filmed 1991, released 1992), Eddie Vedder, Stone Gossard, and Jeff Ament appear as the backing band for fictional singer Cliff Poncier (played by Matt Dillon), in a band called Citizen Dick. Their longest appearance is just over a minute, showing them reading a review of their record. By the time the film was released, Pearl Jam was enormous, which worked greatly in the film's favor. Pearl Jam also contributed two songs to the soundtrack: "Breath" and "State of Love and Trust." "By the time the movie was released in 1992, the band was huge."

Their immense popularity set a high benchmark against which other bands, including Hootie & the Blowfish, were often compared, particularly regarding the power and passion of their lead singer, Eddie Vedder. "Eddie Vetter, the lead singer of Pearl Jam, who by 1993 were basically the biggest band on the charts."

podcast.title: Judgment Night Collaboration with Cypress Hill (1993)
podcast.body: Pearl Jam collaborated with hip-hop outfit Cypress Hill for the 1993 *Judgment Night* soundtrack. This pairing was considered radical at the time due to the limited crossover between rock and hip-hop. The project was a major catalyst for the creation of rap rock and nu metal, and helped bridge the divide between rock and hip-hop fans. "The pairings included Pearl Jam and Cypress Hill, Slayer working with Ice Tea, Faith No More and Buella Tribe, Dinosaur Jr., and Del the Funky Homo sapien, 11 collaborations at all."

podcast.body: Following the death of Kurt Cobain, Pearl Jam's enthusiasm for their 1994 tour waned, leading to the cancellation of the remaining dates. This event occurred amidst their ongoing ticketing dispute with Ticketmaster and shortly before the US Justice Department initiated contact. "Then Kurt Cobain died. podcast.title: 1994 Tour Price Cap Initiative
podcast.body: For their 1994 tour, Pearl Jam actively sought to keep ticket prices as low as possible, a significant stance during the "grunge era." They instructed all promoters to set a ticket face value of $18, with a strict limit of 10% on service charges, meaning the total "all-in" ticket price had to remain under $20. "When it came time to two or in 1994, Pearl Jam told all promoters that they were going to keep ticket prices as low as possible."

podcast.body: Entering 1994, Pearl Jam, alongside Nirvana, was considered among the "unquestioned biggest bands in America," solidifying their dominant position in the music industry. "Going into 1994, Nirvana and Pearl Jam were the unquestioned biggest bands in America."

podcast.title: Eddie Vedder Stalker (1994–1996) – Believed Eddie Was Jesus and Father of Her Children
podcast.body: A mentally ill woman became convinced that all of Eddie's Pearl Jam songs were written about her, that Jesus was the father of her two children via rape, and that Eddie was Jesus — therefore the father of her children. Physical threats were made; fences, security systems, and 24-hour bodyguards were deployed. She ultimately drove her car at 50 mph directly into Eddie's house, forcing him to move to an inaccessible location outside Seattle. Little came of legal proceedings. This explains Eddie's reputation as a recluse during the mid-1990s and is reflected in the song "Lukin." "Eddie ended up with this reputation as a recluse and a hermit, but now you know why."

podcast.title: Eddie Vedder Stalker (1994–1996) – Believed Eddie Was Jesus and Father of Her Children
podcast.body: Between approximately 1994 and 1996, a mentally ill woman became convinced that all of Eddie Vedder's Pearl Jam songs were written personally about her. She also believed that Jesus was the father of her two children via rape, and that Eddie Vedder was Jesus — therefore the father of her children. Physical threats were made, forcing the installation of fences, security systems, and 24-hour bodyguards. Reports indicated she was armed. The situation escalated when she drove her car at 50 mph directly into Eddie's house, at which point he relocated to an inaccessible location outside Seattle. Legal proceedings produced little result. The experience contributed to Eddie's reputation as a recluse and hermit during this period, and is reflected in the song "Lukin" from *No Code* (1996). "Eddie ended up with this reputation as a recluse and a hermit, but now you know why."

podcast.title: Ticketmaster Legal Challenge (1994)
podcast.body: Pearl Jam launched a legal action against Ticketmaster in 1994, aiming to tour with tickets priced below $20 and a service charge no more than $1.80. Ticketmaster refused, stating they needed to charge at least $2 to cover costs. Despite a significant fight, testimony before the U.S. Congress, and an attempt to circumvent Ticketmaster's network, the case accusing Ticketmaster of being anti-competitive collapsed in 1995. The band now uses Ticketmaster for their ticketing. "Despite a good fight, testimony before the U.S. Congress and an attempt to circumvent Ticketmaster's ticket selling network, it didn't work."

podcast.title: Antitrust Hearing and Inconclusive Outcome (June 1995)
podcast.body: A hearing was scheduled for Thursday, June 30, 1995, in Washington D.C., where members of Pearl Jam's organization and supportive music industry figures presented their case against Ticketmaster. Despite intense media coverage, the government's investigation was closed later in 1995 without any substantial action, with only a promise for continued monitoring of the ticketing industry. "But in the end, nothing came of it. The government investigation was closed in 1995 without anyone doing anything."

podcast.body: In the period after their tour cancellation, the US Justice Department contacted Pearl Jam, having monitored Ticketmaster since its 1991 merger with Ticketron and being aware of Pearl Jam's disputes over service charges. The Justice Department reportedly encouraged Pearl Jam to file an antitrust complaint, rather than a lawsuit, initiating an investigation into Ticketmaster's practices. "It appears that the Justice Department may have encouraged Pearl Jam to file a complaint, not a lawsuit, asking for an antitrust investigation into ticket master's practices."

podcast.body: In 2000, Pearl Jam initiated an innovative series of official bootlegs, releasing high-quality, soundboard recordings of their live shows. The first series launched during the Binaural Tour, making 72 shows from North America and Europe available as affordable double-disc CDs and later digital downloads, starting with a Lisbon gig on May 23rd, 2000. "They released a series of official bootlegs, all recorded at the soundboard on tour. The audio was high quality, and the CDs were affordable."

podcast.title: Roskilde 2000 Tragedy
podcast.body: During Pearl Jam's set at Roskilde in 2000, in front of approximately 60,000 people at the Orange Stage, a crowd crush resulted in the death of nine people and 26 injuries. This tragic event led to the implementation of new safety protocols at festivals worldwide. "When nine people died and 26 were injured during Pearl Jam set in front of about 60,000 people at an area called the Orange Stage, that accident set new safety protocols in motion at festivals all over the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Roskilde Festival Crowd Crush (June 30, 2000)
podcast.body: At approximately 10:30 PM on June 30, 2000, 30 minutes into Pearl Jam's set at the Roskilde Festival in Denmark, a group of people fell in a specific area, destabilized by crowd waves on the rain-slicked, muddy ground. This created a void that quickly filled with bodies, leading to the suffocation of nine people within five minutes. In total, nine people died, and 26 were injured, three seriously, with no evidence of drug or severe alcohol use among the victims. "About 30 minutes into the show, a bunch of people fell down all in one specific area, knocked off balance by waves undulating through the crowd on the rain slick muddy ground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Roskilde Festival Tragedy (2000)
podcast.body: On June 30, 2000, Pearl Jam performed at the Roskilde Festival in Denmark during its second day, following heavy rains that left 100,000 attendees soaked and safety concerns that led other bands like The Verve and Pet Shop Boys to cancel. During Pearl Jam's 11:30 PM set, a crowd surge pushed attendees against a steel barrier down a slight, muddy incline. Vocalist Eddie Vedder repeatedly stopped the band, imploring the crowd to move back as the crush became a "slow-motion avalanche of bodies." Ultimately, 26 people were injured, and 8 bodies were pulled from the pile, with another person dying later in hospital. The victims were from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden. "Our lives will never be the same, but we know that this is nothing compared to the grief of the families and friends of those involved."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Roskilde Festival Tragedy (June 30, 2000)
podcast.body: On Friday, June 30, 2000, during Pearl Jam's performance at the Roskilde Festival in Denmark, a crowd surge towards the stage led to a catastrophic crush. Despite Eddie Vedder and the band pleading with the audience to move back, nine people died and countless others were injured when a customized padded barrier failed. This event became one of Europe's worst concert tragedies, leading to the cancellation of the rest of the festival and a police investigation. podcast.title: Roskilde Festival Tragedy (June 30, 2000)

Vocalist Eddie Vedder repeatedly stopped the band, imploring the crowd to move back as the crush became a "slow-motion avalanche of bodies." Ultimately, 26 people were injured, and 8 bodies were pulled from the pile, with another person dying later in hospital. The victims were from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden. podcast.title: "Vs." Anti-System Release Strategy
podcast.body: Pearl Jam deliberately released *Vs.* in stages, with the vinyl edition first appearing in the UK on October 11, 1993, followed by North America on October 12. The CD and cassette versions were delayed until October 18 and 19, respectively. This staggered release was a conscious effort by the band to "mess with the system" and "stick it to the label," Epic Records, which they felt was trying to kill off vinyl in favor of more expensive and profitable CDs. In 1993, none of the band members even owned a CD player, and Jeff Ament preferred a cassette version as his primary listening format. Further challenging the label, the vinyl edition was released without the album title or band name printed on it, forcing Epic to add a sticker to the shrink wrap. "Why? Phil Jim just wanted to mess with the system. So they did. In their mind, it was another way to stick it to the label."

They went to New York for record-deal business, attended a Neil Young concert, were impressed by his long improvisational instrumental jams featuring competing creative visions, and settled on "Pearl Jam." podcast.title: Inspiration for Career Trajectory
podcast.body: Pearl Jam is cited by Billy Talent as a source of inspiration due to their career path, which includes periods of "tremendous success" followed by albums where they "fell off a bit," only to later return with "big splash and great songs and sold out tours." podcast.title: Jeremy Dell's Early Life and Struggles
podcast.body: Jeremy Dell, a 15-year-old from Richardson, Texas, who inspired part of the song "Jeremy," was described as a quiet, sad, but good kid who struggled under a heavy load of problems and could get very angry. He also had a lighter side, enjoying jokes and being a talented artist who won an award for drawing at age seven. Despite appearing to be an ordinary teenager to most, he had previously undergone a psychiatric evaluation and been admitted for a time while attending another school. "People describe Jeremy as a sad kid. He was always very quiet. He was also said to be a good kid, but stuck under a giant load of problems and he could get very angry."

podcast.title: Jeremy Dell's Family Situation and School Transfer
podcast.body: Jeremy Dell changed schools and started at Richardson High on October 16, 1990. His parents had divorced the year before, and he was living with his father and his father's considerably younger girlfriend, while his mother, Wanda, lived elsewhere but remained in regular contact. podcast.body: Pearl Jam was initially viewed critically by Kurt Cobain, who considered them "careerists," too commercial, corporate, and appealing to "jocks." However, Kurt later clarified that the perceived feud was largely his fault and that he should have targeted the record company for pushing Pearl Jam onto the "grunge bandwagon" without their full realization or will. Eddie Vedder now agrees with Kurt's assessment of what was happening to Pearl Jam at the time. "That never was a feud. I slagged them off because I didn't like their band. It was my fault. I should have been slagging off the record company instead of them."

podcast.title: Refusal to Make Videos (After Initial Singles)
podcast.body: After dutifully creating music videos for the first four singles from their debut album *Ten*, Pearl Jam refused to make any more for about six years. This resistance was a significant statement during an era when music videos were considered essential for promotion, reflecting the alt-rock ethos that often expressed disdain for the "We Must Make a Video" practice. "Pearl Jam refused to do any more for about six years."

podcast.title: Return to Ticketmaster for Business Reasons
podcast.body: After their prolonged battles and attempts to use alternative ticketing, Pearl Jam eventually reverted to using Ticketmaster. This decision was driven by changing economic realities in the music industry, as album sales significantly declined by the late 1990s, with revenues dropping from $15-$20 million annually, and illegal file sharing further eroding sales. To compensate for lost album revenue, maximizing income from live touring became essential, which necessitated playing in major venues, most of which had existing ticketing contracts with Ticketmaster. "Well, it was simply the right business decision. In the early 90s, Pearl Jam albums were selling like crazy. So the income stream was fantastic. They were making $15, $20 million a year."

xref.title: Final Concert (August 6, 1996) – The Palace, Hollywood
xref.body: The Ramones played their 2263rd and final gig on August 6, 1996, at The Palace in Hollywood, planned as a celebration of their career. By the 1990s, the band was finally being recognized as pioneers by alternative artists like Pearl Jam, Green Day, and Nirvana. The farewell included dates on the Lollapalooza tour that year, performing alongside Metallica and Soundgarden. Lemmy of Motorhead attended, and Eddie Vedder joined them on stage for their last song, a cover of Dave Clark Five's "Anyway You Want It." The band members simply walked off stage without a farewell speech after the final song. "That final show was on August 6th of 1996. All kinds of people came to pay their respects, including Lemmy of Motorhead."
